findings.title: Denial cache defeats the purpose of fresh requery for newly created resources
findings.body: When the DB requery still returns no grant, a denial is cached for 30s. Permissions for a newly created dashboard or folder can be written after the first Check, for example when the frontend checks before the creator's grant is persisted. In that case every later Check short-circuits on the denial key and never reaches the DB. The creator stays locked out for up to the TTL, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix. Nothing invalidates the denial key when permissions change.

findings.title: Denial cache key collides with permission cache key namespace
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds keys with the same `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey` and joins parts with `_`. UIDs and folder names can themselves contain `_`, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. A denial for one resource can then be applied to another. The two typed caches also share one store, and a key from one can be read by the other and fail to unmarshal. Use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous separator.

findings.title: Denial key uses raw subject UID, not resolved identifier; anonymous/renderer share keys
findings.body: The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` as supplied, which may be a numeric ID or a UID, so one user gets inconsistent keys. Every anonymous subject also maps to one key. The renderer path's denials are cached as well, even though they are static. The permission cache uses the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`, so the denial cache keys should match it.

findings.title: Cached-permission miss always triggers full DB refetch, including for genuinely denied requests on fresh entries
findings.body: Any cached negative result now bypasses the cache and queries the DB, through singleflight but still per request. This lasts until the denial cache absorbs it. For list-like access patterns with many distinct names the denial keys never repeat, so every denied Check costs a DB round trip. Cache hit metrics are also double-counted: a miss is recorded after a cache hit that did not allow.

findings.title: In-proc client caching fully removed
findings.body: The in-proc client now uses a NoopCache, so every authz check goes through the server path. That path does at least the GetUserIdentifiers and permCache lookups plus JSON unmarshal. The earlier 30s client cache may have been hiding a high volume of these calls.
